title: The Life of a Request
subtitle: Trace one page load across the network and find out which hop really costs the most.

objectives.text: Why a new connection costs round trips
How a slow query or a long distance changes it

steps.title: “The store feels slow”
steps.body:
A shopper writes in: the online store feels slow. Before changing anything, find out **where the time goes**.

We'll follow a single page load, from the moment you press Enter until the page is ready, and add up every wait along the way.

callout.text: Loading a page is a chain of short conversations between machines. Each one costs time, and the costs add up.

steps.title: Find the address
steps.body:
Networks deliver to numbers, not names. Your laptop asks a [[dns|DNS]] resolver to turn `store.example` into an [[ip|IP address]].

That's one round trip to a resolver nearby: about **24 ms**.

callout.text: The answer comes with a [[ttl|TTL]], so your laptop and the resolver can reuse it. The next lookup for the same name is usually free.

steps.title: Open a connection
steps.body:
Before any page data moves, the two machines set up a [[tcp|TCP]] connection and then a [[tls|TLS]] session, so nobody along the way can read or change the traffic.

That's two [[rtt|round trips]] to the server. At 35 ms per round trip, **70 ms** pass before your request is even sent.

callout.text: Early in a page load, round trips matter more than bandwidth. [[keep-alive|Reusing a connection]] lets later requests skip this cost.

steps.title: Ask for the page
steps.body:
Now the browser sends `GET /` over the open connection. The request crosses the network, the app code runs for about **12 ms**, and the first bytes head back.

One more round trip plus the work: 35 + 12 = **47 ms**.

steps.title: Fetch the data
steps.body:
The page lists products, so the app asks the [[database]]. App and database sit in the same building, so that trip takes well under a millisecond, but the query itself needs **18 ms**.

Request + server is now 35 + 12 + 18 = **65 ms**.

steps.title: Download the page
steps.body:
Bytes take time to arrive too. The HTML is about 90 KB, and on a typical home connection it finishes arriving about **30 ms** after the first byte.

The browser now has the page text. Total so far: **189 ms**.

steps.title: The rest of the page
steps.body:
The HTML points to stylesheets, scripts and images: 14 more files, about 600 KB. They reuse the open connection and travel side by side, but they still need another round trip and many more bytes.

Download grows to **150 ms**, and the page is ready at about **309 ms**.

callout.text: Of those 309 ms, only about 30 ms is computers working (app + database). Everything else is waiting on the network.

steps.title: Case: one slow query
steps.body:
A new “recommended for you” box ships. Its query reads the whole orders table and takes **420 ms**.

Same network, same handshakes. But request + server jumps from 65 to **467 ms**, and the page now lands at **711 ms**.

callout.text: Measure before you optimize. The fix here is in the database (an [[index]], covered in the Indexes lesson), not a faster network or bigger servers.

steps.title: Case: a shopper far away
steps.body:
Same page, same fast query. But this shopper is in Sydney and the server is in Virginia, so every round trip takes about **190 ms** instead of 35.

The handshakes alone cost 380 ms, each extra round trip for files adds more, and the page needs over **a second**.

callout.text: Cut round trips: reuse connections, use TLS 1.3, and serve files from a [[cdn|CDN]] near the user (covered in the CDN lesson).

steps.title: Where the time went
steps.body:
One page load, four kinds of waiting. Most of the 309 ms was spent moving messages back and forth, not computing.

That's why the rest of this course spends so much time on round trips, distance and caching.

callout.text: Next: what happens when thousands of these requests arrive at once (Latency vs Throughput).

takeaways: DNS turns a name into an address; caching makes repeat lookups almost free.
Every new connection costs round trips before any data moves.
App and database time is often a small slice — until one slow query takes over.
Distance multiplies every round trip, so far-away users feel each one.

panels.title: Where the time went
panels.note: About 30 ms of it is computing.
